questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To be honest I was looking at many different countries, but for some reason South Korea and Yonsei University just seemed to be the most interesting option for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall I loved my time as an exchange student, and I completely fell in love with Korea in my months there, but because I got unlucky with both my housing situation (at first) and got covid, then I can't rate the experience as 10. I would still definetely recommend anyone to go to Korea and attend Yonsei University, which both have a beautiful campus and an amazing location in Sinchon and near Hongdae, but just make better housing decisions than me.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Because of corona everything was online, but we did get some pretty detailed emails with loads of information and The office of international affairs was quick to answer my emails throughout the exchange. But having said that, then there was still things that I didn't know far into my stay, because we never got to have the off-line orientation.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They sent us an email with loads of pdf's and then there was some kind of online game where you could log in an "meet" each other, but because I only received the email the night before, then I didn't get to attend, since the meeting was over before I knew it existed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Because of corona nothing really worked properly, but that will hopefully change.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I got recommended a community by another Dane, which sounded great but was a disaster. The place is called A Home in Sinchon and is run by Jason Shim, and unless you like a dirty apartments and a landlord that doesn't behave in a proper way then you should stay far away. In general I think you should be careful about communities run by a single person - the only other such community I know of, the guy running it supposedly went to jail for breaking the covid laws.
I ended up renting an AirBnb in Hongdae together with two other danes that I met in Korea, and living there was amazing.
Overall I would recommend traveling to Korea early and then rent an Airbnb for a couple of days for when you just arrive. Then when you are there, you can contact different places (AirBnb, goshiwons etc.) and then see the place before paying - in that way you won't get scammed.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
For off-campus living I would recommend staying in Sinchon (where Yonsei is located) or in Hongdae (right next to Sinchon). Both places are very youth friendly, with loads of restaurants, cafes and shopping opportunities.
As I said, then you should be careful to not get scammed, but it is possible to find great places to stay, both rooms alone (AirBnb and goshiwons) and apartments to share (Airbnb or facebook groups, where other people already have found an apartment and are looking for other exchange students to rent the other rooms).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I never tried to apply for on-campus housing, since I didn't like all the rules that came with it (something about curfew and limitations on guests), but I do know a few people that stayed on campus and they seemed happy about it.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: When you first read the manual as to how you apply, it seems very confusing, but it works alright and I ended up with all the classes I wanted

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
They will give you an extensive manual as to how to apply, and if you follow that it is easy enough.
Long story short, at first there is a bidding round where you get 72 points and then you can bid on the different courses you want (here it doesn't matter when in the period you apply). If you don't get the courses you want in the first round, then there is a second round where you can apply for remaining spots (here it is the first to register that gets the spot). It is the same principle in the add/drop period.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I think you could probably write to the office of international affairs, but it wasn't necessary for me. If you don't get into a class, or want to register for a class that isn't normally allowed for exchange students, then it is possible that the professors teaching the course can help you.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I ended up with all the classes I wanted. I got Virus and Host and Immunology in the first bidding round, and Cancer biology in the add/drop period (since it isn't normally available for exchange students, I had to write an email to be registered).
I always wanted a course about Korean culture, but I ended up not getting the one I first applied for. I was still allowed to participate in the first class, where I ended up not liking the professor. I then applied for another Korean culture class in the second round of registration, which I then got.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be sure to know which classes you want to apply for, and check what mileage (points) people in the previous years bid - this will give you some kind of idea as to how many points you should bid.
If you don't get the courses you want in the first round, then be sure to be ready for exactly when the next round opens - the spots could be gone in a couple of minutes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A big 4 out of 5

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took biomedicine courses on level 3000 and 4000, both of which were appropriate in level. 
The lectures and books were on the same level as at KU (in Immunology we used the same book as is used here in DK), but to me it seemed as if even though the exams were on that same level, then they were more lenient on the grading than here in DK.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At Yonsei each 3 credit course has 3 hours of lectures each week. There isn't any problem solving/SAU classes, but it is a bit different from professor to professor how the lectures go. Some will talk the entire time (Virus and Host), some will have questions and involve the students in the lectures (Immunology to some extend but mostly Cancer biology) and in some there are lectures and then discussion between the students (Korean Food and Culture).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I took 4 courses, where 3 were related to my studies and then 1 about Korea:
Cancer biology (LST4002)
Immunology (BTE3403)
Virus and Host (BTE4610)
Korean Food and Culture (IEE2084)
For other students I would recommend taking either 3 or 4 courses, since I was quite busy at times and there is so much to explore in Korea outside of university

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I liked all my courses. While Korean food and culture didn't have anything to do with molecular biomedicine, I still found it really interesting and fun (although I did end up spending more time on it than I expected). 
Cancer biology was probably my favourite course, and even though it isn't normally available for exchange students then if it isn't filled up, you can write the professor and ask for permission (and he's really nice). Virus and host was also really interesting.
Immunology was the course I had the hardest time with, since the professor isn't very good. If you want to have an Immunology course I would recommend reading in advance, otherwise it is pretty hard to follow along with his lectures.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: In my first apartment I had to pay for everything in advance, and then when I wanted to move, he wouldn't give me the remaining months back. I therefore ended up spending about 10,000 DKK more on housing than I expected (but this isn't a part of the 4000 DKK I wrote for housing).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
As everybody else will tell you, fruit and vegetables are very expensive in Korea (I would recommend finding street vendors that sell them - then the price is reasonable).
Going out eating in restaurants is really cheap compared to DK, but since I ended up going out for both lunch and dinner, it still cost a lot of money overall. If you want to spend less on food then I recommend to eat lunch from the cafeteria at Yonsei, from convenience stores or finding other cheap places (Boxsquare close to Yonsei have many cheap options) and to not going to as many cafes as I did .

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Because of corona, Yonsei didn't have anything available when I was on exchange. The only thing I know was possible was the buddy programme, but I didn't receive any information about it before it was too late to apply, but I would have applied if possible.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think Yonsei outside of corona have some interesting programmes, so check that out, but otherwise just go out and explore the city and country.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
See as much of South Korea as possible. 
Seoul is a wonderful city with so many different things to see, so go out and eat amazing food from restaurants and cafes (their cafe culture is amazing), go to museums, palaces, temples and parks or just go around and explore a certain area (or mountain) and I assure you every day will be filled. 
Trips outside of Seoul is also a must. I visited Busan (Songdo marine cable car, Gamcheon village,  Haeddong Yonggungsa temple and Gwangalli and Haeundae beach), Jeju (Udo Island, Hallasan mountain, O'sulloc tea museum, Seogwipo city, etc.), Incheon (Chinatown and Wolmido), DMZ and Sokcho/Seoraksan National park (visit when the leaves change colour. The trip to Ulsan bawi is the most popular, but Geumganggul cave is the most beautiful trek).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Although I haven't been to Korea before, I have been to other places in Asia in my gap year, which might have been a factor in not experiencing any culture shocks. 
You have to get used to it being difficult to interact with many locals, since their English isn't the best, but it still always worked out.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Because we weren't allowed in-class lectures, then I didn't socialize very much with local students. The few I got to meet were other exchange students' buddies, so I guess the buddy programme is a good way to start.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Other than the language barrier then there wasn't really anything that was challenging

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: All of it - from how many old traditions are still kept alive to how new and modern so much of the country is. Everything from the busy cities to the peaceful nature was amazing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't be afraid to find accommodation after you have arrived, just arrive early
2. If possible, plan your classes so you can have a long weekend and go on trips (I personally only had classes monday-wednesday)
3. Everyone is there to get new friends, so be open minded

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No - just enjoy your stay!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know and live in another country

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My housing situation and getting covid and spending a week in a government quarantine facility on the other side of the country

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
